pos: n. (one journeying; the guest Job received, the figure in Nathan's parable, and the men who kept to byways when the highways were unsafe)
etymology: From travel, originally the same word as travail — French travail, labour — because a journey was hard work. The Hebrew terms are helek, one who walks, and orach, one on a road.
biblical_def: Deborah's song dates the disorder of the period by what happened to travel: “In the days of Shamgar the son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were unoccupied, and the travellers walked through byways” (Judges 5:6). Empty roads are the mark of a lawless country. Nathan puts a traveller at the centre of the parable that broke David: “And there came a traveller unto the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock and of his own herd, to dress for the wayfaring man that was come unto him; but took the poor man's lamb” (2 Samuel 12:4). The whole force of the parable rests on a duty everyone in that culture assumed — a guest must be fed — and on the rich man discharging it at his neighbour's expense. Job cites the same duty as evidence of his integrity: “The stranger did not lodge in the street: but I opened my doors to the traveller” (Job 31:32). And Jeremiah dares to use the image of God Himself, in a complaint: “why shouldest thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man that turneth aside to tarry for a night?” (Jeremiah 14:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a traveller as one who travels in any way, and notes that travel and travail are the same word, a journey being laborious.
webster_full: TRAVELLER, n. One who travels in any way.
2. One who visits foreign countries.
TRAVEL, v.i. To journey; to walk or ride to a distant place.
WAYFARING, a. Travelling; passing; being on a journey.
HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 12:4

And there came a traveller unto the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock and of his own herd, to dress for the wayfaring man that was come unto him; but took the poor man's lamb, and dressed it for the man that was come to him.
The stranger did not lodge in the street: but I opened my doors to the traveller.
Judges 5:6
In the days of Shamgar the son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were unoccupied, and the travellers walked through byways.
Jeremiah 14:8
O the hope of Israel, the saviour thereof in time of trouble, why shouldest thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man that turneth aside to tarry for a night?
corruption_summary: Hospitality is reduced to entertaining friends in a tidy house, and Scripture means opening a door to a stranger who cannot repay.
corruption_paragraphs: The biblical duty concerns the traveller — a person passing through, unknown, unable to return the favour. Job's boast is that the stranger did not lodge in the street; the elder must be given to hospitality; the Hebrews are told to entertain strangers, since some have entertained angels unawares. Modern hospitality has narrowed almost entirely to hosting people one already knows, in circumstances one controls, which is a good thing and is not the thing commanded. The narrowing has a cost. A congregation that has lost the practice of receiving strangers has also lost the setting in which most of the New Testament's one-another commands were originally obeyed.

Nathan's parable rewards a second look. The rich man was not condemned for refusing hospitality — he provided the meal — but for providing it out of the poor man's flock. Generosity funded by someone else's loss is the precise shape of the sin, which is why David's anger was so hot and Nathan's thou art the man so devastating. The pattern survives wherever an institution or a leader builds a reputation for care on resources extracted from those least able to spare them. The parable was aimed at a king who had taken a man's only wife, and it was framed as a story about a lamb and a guest.
roots_summary: Hebrew helek, a traveller — 2 Samuel 12:4; orach, a wayfarer — Judges 5:6, Job 31:32; arach, to wander or journey — Jeremiah 14:8.
roots_lines: Hebrew helek — one who walks, a traveller; 2 Samuel 12:4, its notable occurrence in Nathan's parable.
Hebrew orach — a path, and one who travels it; Judges 5:6 and Job 31:32.
Hebrew netibah — a byway, a crooked path; Judges 5:6, where travellers avoided the highways.
Hebrew ger — a stranger, sojourner; Job 31:32, the man Job would not leave in the street.
Hebrews 13:2 states the standing duty: be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
usage: “The travellers walked through byways” — empty highways are the mark of a lawless land.
“I opened my doors to the traveller” — Job's evidence of integrity.
The rich man fed the guest, and fed him out of the poor man's flock.

pos: adj. (using the left hand; of Ehud the deliverer, and of the seven hundred Benjamite slingers who could not miss)
etymology: From left and handed. The Hebrew is a striking idiom: itter yad-yemino, bound or restricted as to the right hand — the left-hander is described by what his right hand cannot do.
biblical_def: “But when the children of Israel cried unto the LORD, the LORD raised them up a deliverer, Ehud the son of Gera, a Benjamite, a man lefthanded: and by him the children of Israel sent a present unto Eglon the king of Moab” (Judges 3:15). The detail is not decoration. A guard searching a man for weapons would check the left thigh, where a right-handed man wears his dagger; Ehud had made a two-edged dagger and “did gird it under his raiment upon his right thigh” and walked in armed. The narrative pays the detail off: “And Ehud put forth his left hand, and took the dagger from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly” (Judges 3:21). The same trait reappears as a tribal military speciality: “Among all this people there were seven hundred chosen men lefthanded; every one could sling stones at an hair breadth, and not miss” (Judges 20:16). There is an irony in it, since Benjamin means son of the right hand. The tribe named for the right hand produced the nation's left-handed fighters, and God's deliverer was a man whose disadvantage was the thing that got him past the guards.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines left-handed as having the left hand more strong and dexterous than the right, and left-handedness as habitual use of the left hand.
webster_full: LEFT-HANDED, a. Having the left hand or arm more strong and dexterous than the right; using the left hand and arm with more dexterity than the right.
LEFT-HANDEDNESS, n. Habitual use of the left hand, or rather the ability to use the left hand with more ease and strength than the right.
DELIVERER, n. One who delivers or rescues; a preserver.
SLING, n. An instrument for throwing stones, consisting of a strap and two strings.
DAGGER, n. A short sword; a poniard.
scriptures: Judges 3:15

But when the children of Israel cried unto the LORD, the LORD raised them up a deliverer, Ehud the son of Gera, a Benjamite, a man lefthanded: and by him the children of Israel sent a present unto Eglon the king of Moab.
Judges 3:21
And Ehud put forth his left hand, and took the dagger from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly:
Judges 20:16
Among all this people there were seven hundred chosen men lefthanded; every one could sling stones at an hair breadth, and not miss.
Judges 3:19
But he himself turned again from the quarries that were by Gilgal, and said, I have a secret errand unto thee, O king: who said, Keep silence. And all that stood by him went out from him.
corruption_summary: The narrative details of the historical books are treated as incidental colour, and here the whole deliverance turns on one of them.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's incidental details are load-bearing. A reader skimming Judges 3 sees an odd biographical note; a reader attending to it sees why the assassination worked. The Hebrew idiom — restricted as to the right hand — describes the trait as a limitation, and the limitation is exactly what carried a weapon past a search. God's habit of using what men count a disadvantage runs from Moses' slow speech to Paul's thorn, and the doctrine is stated plainly: God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.

The second observation concerns the tribe. Benjamin means son of the right hand, and Benjamin produced seven hundred left-handed slingers who could hit a hair's breadth. Judges 20 is a grim chapter — those slingers were used in a civil war provoked by an atrocity at Gibeah — and the same skill that made Ehud a deliverer nearly destroyed the tribe. Gift is not virtue. The book of Judges records repeatedly that men raised up for deliverance were capable of terrible things, and it does so without flattening the record, because the point of the book is not the quality of the judges but the mercy of the God who kept raising them up.
roots_summary: Hebrew itter yad-yemino, bound as to the right hand — Judges 3:15, 20:16; Benjamin, son of the right hand; qela, a sling — Judges 20:16.
roots_lines: Hebrew itter — shut up, bound, restricted; in the idiom itter yad-yemino, restricted as to his right hand.
Hebrew Binyamin — son of the right hand; Genesis 35:18, the name Jacob gave in place of Benoni.
Hebrew qela — a sling; Judges 20:16, the weapon of the seven hundred, and David's in 1 Samuel 17.
Hebrew Ehud — the second judge, of the tribe of Benjamin; Judges 3:15-30.
1 Corinthians 1:27 gives the doctrine the detail illustrates: God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
usage: “A man lefthanded” — and the guards searched the wrong thigh.
“Seven hundred chosen men lefthanded; every one could sling stones at an hair breadth”.
The tribe named son of the right hand produced the nation's left-handers.

pos: v. and n. (to press about in a crowd; what the multitudes did to Christ, and the contrast Scripture draws between pressing and touching)
etymology: Old English gethrang, a crowd, from a root meaning to press. The Greek thlibo means to squeeze or compress — the same verb rendered tribulation elsewhere; sunthlibo is to press on all sides.
biblical_def: The crowds around the Lord were physically dangerous. “And he spake to his disciples, that a small ship should wait on him because of the multitude, lest they should throng him” (Mark 3:9) — a boat kept ready offshore so He would not be crushed. On the way to Jairus's house, “much people followed him, and thronged him” (Mark 5:24), and Luke records the same pressure (Luke 8:42). Then the woman with the issue of blood touched the border of His garment, and the Lord asked who touched Him. Peter's reply is one of the most instructive sentences in the Gospels: “Master, the multitude throng thee and press thee, and sayest thou, Who touched me?” (Luke 8:45). Hundreds were touching Him; one had touched Him. The Lord answers, “Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me” (Luke 8:46). The distinction is exact and it is the doctrinal centre of the episode: proximity is not contact, and a crowd pressing against Christ is not the same thing as one trembling hand laid on Him in faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines throng as a crowd, a multitude of persons or living beings pressing or pressed into a close body, and to throng as to crowd or press.
webster_full: THRONG, n. A crowd; a multitude of persons or of living beings pressing or pressed into a close body or assemblage.
THRONG, v.t. To crowd or press, as persons; to oppress or annoy with a crowd of living beings.
THRONG, v.i. To crowd together; to press into a close body, as a multitude of persons.
PRESS, v.t. To urge with force or weight; to squeeze; to crush.
MULTITUDE, n. The state of being many; a great number collectively.
scriptures: Luke 8:45
And Jesus said, Who touched me? When all denied, Peter and they that were with him said, Master, the multitude throng thee and press thee, and sayest thou, Who touched me?
Luke 8:46
And Jesus said, Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me.
Mark 5:24
And Jesus went with him; and much people followed him, and thronged him.
Mark 3:9
And he spake to his disciples, that a small ship should wait on him because of the multitude, lest they should throng him.
corruption_summary: Crowds are treated as the measure of a ministry, and the Gospels use them to teach the difference between pressing and believing.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 8:45 ought to be read at every meeting where attendance is discussed. The multitude thronged and pressed Him; Peter thought the question absurd; and the Lord distinguished one woman's touch from the contact of hundreds. Numbers are not nothing — the Gospels record them, and Acts counts the three thousand — but they are not the measure. The crowds that thronged Him in Galilee had largely gone by John 6, when the teaching grew hard, and He let them go and asked the twelve whether they would also leave. A ministry that reads its crowd as its verdict has adopted a standard the Lord Himself declined to use.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the woman's faith and how little of it she had. She came behind Him, believing she must not be seen, holding a superstitious-sounding notion that touching His clothes would be enough, and unwilling to ask. Her theology was thin and her courage was less. And virtue went out of Him, and He called her daughter, and told her that her faith had made her whole. Faith is not made effectual by its strength or its precision but by its object, and this passage is the plainest illustration in the Gospels — a trembling and half-informed touch received what an entire pressing crowd did not.
roots_summary: Greek thlibo (G2346), to press or squeeze — Mark 3:9; sunthlibo (G4918), to press on all sides — Mark 5:24, 5:31; sunecho (G4912) and apothlibo (G598) — Luke 8:45.
roots_lines: Greek thlibo (G2346) — to press, afflict; Mark 3:9, and the root of thlipsis, tribulation.
Greek sunthlibo (G4918) — to press together from all sides; Mark 5:24 and 5:31, of the crowd about Christ.
Greek apothlibo (G598) — to squeeze, crush; Luke 8:45, its only occurrence.
Greek haptomai (G680) — to touch, to fasten oneself to; the woman's verb in Luke 8:44-47.
Luke 8:48 gives the Lord's verdict: Daughter, be of good comfort: thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace.
usage: “The multitude throng thee and press thee, and sayest thou, Who touched me?”
“Somebody hath touched me: for I perceive that virtue is gone out of me”.
Hundreds were touching Him; one had touched Him.

pos: v.t. and adj. (to subdue or domesticate; used of the Gadarene whom no man could bind, and of the tongue which no man can tame)
etymology: Old English tam, domesticated. The Greek damazo means to subdue or break in, used of animals and of men — and in James of the one member of the body that resists it.
biblical_def: Mark uses the word of the man among the tombs: “Because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces: neither could any man tame him” (Mark 5:4). Every restraint had been tried and had failed — and the Lord delivered him with a word, and he was found sitting, clothed, and in his right mind. James applies the same verb to something nearer home: “For every kind of beasts, and of birds, and of serpents, and of things in the sea, is tamed, and hath been tamed of mankind: But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison” (James 3:7-8). The argument moves from the greater to the lesser and lands on an absurdity: man has subdued every order of creature and cannot govern one small member of his own body. James has already said why: “the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity… and it is set on fire of hell” (James 3:6). And he names the specific inconsistency: “Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God” (James 3:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tame as having lost its native wildness and shyness, domestic, and to tame as to reclaim or subdue.
webster_full: TAME, a. Having lost its native wildness and shyness; domestic; gentle.
2. Crushed; subdued; depressed; spiritless.
TAME, v.t. To reclaim; to reduce from a wild to a domestic state; to make gentle and familiar.
2. To subdue; to conquer; to depress; as, to tame the pride of men.
UNRULY, a. Disregarding restraint; licentious; disposed to violate laws; turbulent; ungovernable.
scriptures: James 3:8
But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison.
James 3:7
For every kind of beasts, and of birds, and of serpents, and of things in the sea, is tamed, and hath been tamed of mankind:
James 3:9
Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God.
Mark 5:4
Because that he had been often bound with fetters and chains, and the chains had been plucked asunder by him, and the fetters broken in pieces: neither could any man tame him.
corruption_summary: Sins of speech are ranked as minor, and James makes the tongue the test of whether a man's religion is real at all.
corruption_paragraphs: James has already said that a man who seems to be religious and bridleth not his tongue deceives his own heart, and that his religion is vain. That is an extraordinary weight to place on speech, and it is out of all proportion to how the matter is usually treated. Gossip, slander, contempt, the cutting remark, the anonymous comment — these are the ordinary sins of respectable congregations, and they are rarely disciplined and seldom confessed. James calls the tongue a fire, a world of iniquity, set on fire of hell. A church that would remove a man for drunkenness and tolerate a lifetime of destructive speech has not weighed the epistle it reads.

The two texts together supply the answer to the despair James's words might otherwise produce. No man can tame the tongue — and neither could any man tame the Gadarene, until One came who was not merely a man. The chains had all failed and the Lord spoke and the man sat clothed and in his right mind. James is not saying the tongue cannot be governed; he is saying no man can do it, which drives the reader to the only One who can. The remedy is not a technique of self-control but the same power that emptied a legion out of a man among the tombs, and it works on the heart, since out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.
roots_summary: Greek damazo (G1150), to tame or subdue — Mark 5:4, James 3:7-8; akatascheton (G183), unruly — James 3:8; chalinagogeo (G5468), to bridle — James 1:26.
roots_lines: Greek damazo (G1150) — to subdue, tame; Mark 5:4 of the Gadarene, and James 3:7-8 of beasts and of the tongue.
Greek akatascheton (G183) — that cannot be restrained; James 3:8, its only occurrence.
Greek chalinagogeo (G5468) — to lead with a bridle; James 1:26 and 3:2, the figure James prefers for speech.
Greek homoiosis (G3669) — similitude, likeness; James 3:9, men made after the similitude of God — the reason cursing them is monstrous.
Matthew 12:34 locates the root: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.
usage: “The tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil” — and no man could tame the Gadarene either.
“Therewith bless we God… and therewith curse we men” — the same mouth.
Every order of creature subdued, and one small member ungoverned.

pos: n. (a learner or pupil; in Chronicles the singer under instruction, and in Malachi one half of a phrase for a whole household)
etymology: Latin scholaris, from schola, a school. In 1611 a scholar is a pupil, not a savant — the modern sense of an accomplished academic is a later drift, and the Authorized Version means the learner.
biblical_def: David's organisation of the temple singers assigns duties by lot with a striking evenness: “And they cast lots, ward against ward, as well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar” (1 Chronicles 25:8). Two hundred and eighty-eight men were instructed in the songs of the LORD (1 Chronicles 25:7), and the lot did not distinguish master from learner. The other use is a judgment formula: “The LORD will cut off the man that doeth this, the master and the scholar, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and him that offereth an offering unto the LORD of hosts” (Malachi 2:12). The sin in view is named in the previous verse — Judah “hath married the daughter of a strange god” (Malachi 2:11) — and the phrase the master and the scholar is an idiom of totality, like root and branch: the whole line, teacher and taught together, cut off. Both texts assume the ordinary arrangement of biblical learning, which is a named teacher with named pupils, in a trade or a craft or the songs of the LORD, and not a solitary reader with a book.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a scholar as one who learns of a teacher, a pupil or disciple, and secondarily a man of letters.
webster_full: SCHOLAR, n. One who learns of a teacher; one who is under the tuition of a preceptor; a pupil; a disciple; a learner; a student.
2. A man of letters.
3. Emphatically, a man eminent for erudition; a person of high attainments in science or literature.
4. A pedant; a man of books.
DISCIPLE, n. A learner; a scholar; one who receives or professes to receive instruction from another.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 25:8
And they cast lots, ward against ward, as well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar.
Malachi 2:12
The LORD will cut off the man that doeth this, the master and the scholar, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and him that offereth an offering unto the LORD of hosts.
1 Chronicles 25:7
So the number of them, with their brethren that were instructed in the songs of the LORD, even all that were cunning, was two hundred fourscore and eight.
Malachi 2:11

Judah hath dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Judah hath profaned the holiness of the LORD which he loved, and hath married the daughter of a strange god.
corruption_summary: Learning is imagined as a solitary transaction with information, and Scripture assumes a teacher, a pupil, and a shared work.
corruption_paragraphs: The Authorized Version's scholar is a learner sitting under a teacher, and the pairing the teacher as the scholar assumes a relation rather than an achievement. Modern learning, and modern Christian learning in particular, is largely conducted alone — a reader, a screen, a library of opinions selected by the reader himself. What is lost is not information, which has never been more available, but the correction that only a known teacher in a real congregation can administer. Discipleship in the New Testament is this same shape: named men taught by a named apostle, in company, over years, with their errors addressed by someone with the standing to address them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the levelling in 1 Chronicles 25:8. The lots were cast as well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar — the master singer and the apprentice took their turns by the same lot. Ministry rosters are not usually built this way, and the instinct to reserve the significant slots for the accomplished is strong and looks like wisdom. David's arrangement placed the learner and the master under the same providence, which is one of the ways a learner becomes a master and one of the ways a master is kept from thinking himself indispensable.
roots_summary: Hebrew talmid, a scholar or pupil — 1 Chronicles 25:8, its only occurrence in the Old Testament; anah in the idiom of Malachi 2:12; bin, to instruct — 1 Chronicles 25:7.
roots_lines: Hebrew talmid — a pupil, scholar; 1 Chronicles 25:8, its only Old Testament occurrence, and the root of the later talmid chakham.
Hebrew bin — to discern, and in the causative to instruct; 1 Chronicles 25:7, of those instructed in the songs of the LORD.
Hebrew er veoneh — the waker and the answerer; the idiom of Malachi 2:12 rendered the master and the scholar.
Hebrew mebin — a teacher, one who causes to understand; the counterpart of the scholar in 1 Chronicles 25:8.
2 Timothy 2:2 gives the New Testament chain: the things thou hast heard of me… commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
usage: “As well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar” — the same lot for both.
“The master and the scholar” — an idiom for a whole line cut off.
In 1611 a scholar is a pupil, not an expert.

pos: n. (a public speaker or advocate; Tertullus who prosecuted Paul, and the eloquent orator listed among the props God removes from a nation)
etymology: Latin orator, a speaker or pleader, from orare, to speak or plead. The Greek in Acts 24:1 is rhetor — a professional advocate hired to plead a case before a court.
biblical_def: Isaiah lists the supports God removes when He judges a nation: after the mighty man, the judge, the prophet and the prudent comes “The captain of fifty, and the honourable man, and the counsellor, and the cunning artificer, and the eloquent orator” (Isaiah 3:3). Skilled public speech is counted among the stays of a society, along with bread and water (Isaiah 3:1) — and it is removed. The New Testament gives the profession a face. “And after five days Ananias the high priest descended with the elders, and with a certain orator named Tertullus, who informed the governor against Paul” (Acts 24:1). His opening is preserved, and it is pure flattery: “Seeing that by thee we enjoy great quietness, and that very worthy deeds are done unto this nation by thy providence” (Acts 24:2) — addressed to Felix, whose administration was notorious. The Sanhedrin, unable to make its case, hired a professional to make it sound better. Paul's reply begins without compliment and rests on facts anyone could check. The contrast between the two speeches is the chapter's quiet argument.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an orator as a public speaker, in ancient Rome a professional pleader of causes, and one who is eloquent.
webster_full: ORATOR, n. A public speaker.
2. In ancient Rome, a public speaker or pleader of causes in courts.
3. A man of eloquence; an eloquent speaker.
4. In modern usage, a person who pronounces a discourse publicly on some special occasion.
FLATTERY, n. False praise; commendation bestowed for the purpose of gaining favor.
scriptures: Acts 24:1
And after five days Ananias the high priest descended with the elders, and with a certain orator named Tertullus, who informed the governor against Paul.
Acts 24:2
And when he was called forth, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying, Seeing that by thee we enjoy great quietness, and that very worthy deeds are done unto this nation by thy providence,
Isaiah 3:3
The captain of fifty, and the honourable man, and the counsellor, and the cunning artificer, and the eloquent orator.
Isaiah 3:1
For, behold, the Lord, the LORD of hosts, doth take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the stay and the staff, the whole stay of bread, and the whole stay of water,
corruption_summary: Eloquence is treated as evidence of a case, and Acts 24 puts a hired rhetorician and a plain-speaking prisoner side by side to show the difference.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke preserves the opening of Tertullus's speech, and the preservation is deliberate. Felix was a governor whose corruption is attested outside Scripture and shows in the chapter itself — he kept Paul two years hoping for a bribe. Tertullus praises his providence and the great quietness the nation enjoys under him. That is flattery in its exact biblical sense: false praise offered to gain favour, and Proverbs says a man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet. Paul's answer opens with a single measured sentence of civility and then goes straight to what can be verified: it is but twelve days since he went up to worship, and they neither found him disputing in the temple nor raising up the people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isaiah's estimate of eloquence, which is neither the modern contempt for rhetoric nor the modern captivity to it. The eloquent orator is listed among a nation's genuine supports — alongside the judge, the counsellor and the skilled craftsman — and his removal is a judgment. Public speech well used holds a society together; the ability to state a case clearly is a gift of God and its loss is a real loss. And the same Scriptures show a hired tongue serving a corrupt court, so the gift is measured by what it is used for. Paul, who declined the excellency of speech, could plead before governors and kings for years without losing the thread.
roots_summary: Greek rhetor (G4489), a public pleader — Acts 24:1, its only occurrence; Hebrew nebon lachash, skilled in charm or speech — Isaiah 3:3.
roots_lines: Greek rhetor (G4489) — an orator, a professional advocate; Acts 24:1, its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Hebrew nebon lachash — discerning in whispering or enchantment; Isaiah 3:3, rendered the eloquent orator.
Hebrew mashen umashenah — the stay and the staff; Isaiah 3:1, the supports God removes.
Greek Tertullus — the advocate hired by the Sanhedrin; Acts 24:1-8.
1 Corinthians 2:1 gives Paul's own practice: I came not with excellency of speech or of wisdom, declaring unto you the testimony of God.
usage: “A certain orator named Tertullus, who informed the governor against Paul”.
“Seeing that by thee we enjoy great quietness” — said to Felix, of all men.
“The eloquent orator” — listed among a nation's supports, and removed in judgment.

pos: n. (a place of public assembly and spectacle; the great theatre at Ephesus into which the rioting city rushed)
etymology: Greek theatron, a place for viewing, from theaomai, to behold. In a Greek city the theatre served as the venue for the public assembly as well as for performance, which is why a riot ended there.
biblical_def: Demetrius the silversmith, whose trade in shrines of Diana was suffering, raised the city: “And the whole city was filled with confusion: and having caught Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul's companions in travel, they rushed with one accord into the theatre” (Acts 19:29). Luke then records two things about the crowd and one about Paul. The crowd: “Some therefore cried one thing, and some another: for the assembly was confused; and the more part knew not wherefore they were come together” (Acts 19:32) — as concise an account of a mob as has ever been written. Paul wanted to go in and speak, “and the disciples suffered him not” (Acts 19:30), and “certain of the chief of Asia, which were his friends, sent unto him, desiring him that he would not adventure himself into the theatre” (Acts 19:31). The riot was quieted not by an apostle but by the town clerk, who pointed out that the courts were open and deputies available, and warned that the city was in danger of being called to account for the uproar (Acts 19:40) — and dismissed the assembly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a theatre as a house for the exhibition of dramatic performances, and among the ancients an edifice in which spectacles were exhibited to the people.
webster_full: THEATRE, n. Among the Greeks and Romans, an edifice in which spectacles or shows were exhibited for the amusement of spectators.
2. In modern times, a house for the exhibition of dramatic performances.
3. A place rising by steps or gradations like the seats of a theater.
4. A place of action or exhibition; as the theater of the war.
ASSEMBLY, n. A company or collection of individuals in the same place; usually for the same purpose.
scriptures: Acts 19:29
And the whole city was filled with confusion: and having caught Gaius and Aristarchus, men of Macedonia, Paul's companions in travel, they rushed with one accord into the theatre.
Acts 19:32
Some therefore cried one thing, and some another: for the assembly was confused; and the more part knew not wherefore they were come together.
Acts 19:31
And certain of the chief of Asia, which were his friends, sent unto him, desiring him that he would not adventure himself into the theatre.
Acts 19:30
And when Paul would have entered in unto the people, the disciples suffered him not.
corruption_summary: Opposition to the gospel is assumed to be principled, and Luke shows a riot driven by trade and sustained by people who did not know why they had come.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 19 is the most clear-eyed account of a mob in ancient literature. The stated cause was the honour of Diana; the actual cause is given in Demetrius's own speech to his fellow craftsmen — by this craft we have our wealth, and it is in danger. Beneath that, the crowd shouted for two hours without most of them knowing what the matter was: the more part knew not wherefore they were come together. Christians facing hostility are often tempted to assume a coherent ideological opponent, and sometimes there is one. Frequently there is a threatened interest, a practised agitator, and a great many people carried along who could not state the question.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Paul's submission to counsel. He wanted to go in — two of his companions were inside — and the disciples would not let him, and friends among the officials of the province urged him not to. He stayed out. The same man walked back into Lystra the day after being stoned and later sailed to Jerusalem against the pleading of every church on the route, so this was not timidity and not a rule. It was a judgment made in company rather than alone. A courageous man who cannot be restrained by the brethren is not more courageous; he has simply removed the checks God has put around him.
roots_summary: Greek theatron (G2302), a theatre or spectacle — Acts 19:29, 19:31, 1 Corinthians 4:9; ekklesia (G1577), assembly — Acts 19:32, 19:39, 19:41.
roots_lines: Greek theatron (G2302) — a place of viewing; Acts 19:29 and 19:31 of the building, 1 Corinthians 4:9 of the apostles as a spectacle.
Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly, the word elsewhere rendered church; used in Acts 19 of a rioting civic gathering and of the lawful assembly.
Greek sugchusis (G4799) — confusion; Acts 19:29, its only occurrence.
Greek Asiarches (G775) — chief of Asia; Acts 19:31, provincial officials who were Paul's friends.
Acts 19:40 records the town clerk's warning: we are in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar.
usage: “They rushed with one accord into the theatre” — the venue of the public assembly.
“The more part knew not wherefore they were come together”.
“The disciples suffered him not” — and he stayed out.

pos: n. (a contest or struggle; Paul's word for the strain of his ministry, including for churches he had never met)
etymology: Latin conflictus, from confligere, to strike together. The Greek is agon — the athletic contest, the arena — from which come agonize and agony. It denotes a struggle entered deliberately, not an accident.
biblical_def: Paul tells the Philippians that their sufferings are the same as his: they are “Having the same conflict which ye saw in me, and now hear to be in me” (Philippians 1:30). The preceding verse establishes how he regards such suffering: “For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake” (Philippians 1:29). Suffering is given — the word is the ordinary one for a gift of grace. The second use reveals something about pastoral labour that is easily missed: “For I would that ye knew what great conflict I have for you, and for them at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh” (Colossians 2:1). Paul is in prison, and his agon is on behalf of congregations he has never visited. The aim is stated next: “That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding” (Colossians 2:2). The conflict is largely prayer and largely unseen, and he wants them to know it is happening.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conflict as a striking or dashing against each other, a fighting, a contest, and a struggle or clashing of opposing principles.
webster_full: CONFLICT, n. A striking or dashing against each other, as of two moving bodies in opposition; violent collision of substances.
2. A fighting; combat, as between men, and applicable to individuals or to armies.
3. Contention; strife; contest.
4. A struggling with difficulties; a striving to oppose or overcome.
AGONY, n. In strictness, the pain of contest; extreme pain of body or mind; anguish.
scriptures: Philippians 1:30
Having the same conflict which ye saw in me, and now hear to be in me.
Colossians 2:1
For I would that ye knew what great conflict I have for you, and for them at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my face in the flesh;
Philippians 1:29
For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake;
Colossians 2:2

That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ;
corruption_summary: The Christian life is presented as a resolution of conflict, and Paul presents conflict as part of what is given along with faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Philippians 1:29 is among the least quoted verses in evangelistic preaching, and it belongs in it. To the Philippians it is given — graciously granted, the word used for a favour bestowed — not only to believe on Christ but also to suffer for His sake. Both are gifts. Presentations of the gospel that promise the resolution of a convert's difficulties are not merely optimistic; they contradict the terms the apostles stated openly, and they produce believers who conclude at the first hard season that something has gone wrong. Paul's pastoral practice was the opposite: he returned to the cities where he had been stoned and driven out, confirming the souls of the disciples and telling them that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Colossians 2:1. Paul, a prisoner, describes a great agon — the word for an athlete's contest — carried on for congregations at Colosse and Laodicea whose faces he had never seen. That is a description of intercession, and it is labour rather than sentiment. Two things follow. Prayer for people one will never meet is real work and Scripture treats it as such. And a minister's hardest labour is frequently invisible to the people it is for, which is why Paul thought it worth telling them — I would that ye knew.
roots_summary: Greek agon (G73), a contest or struggle — Philippians 1:30, Colossians 2:1, 1 Timothy 6:12, Hebrews 12:1; the root of agonizomai (G75), to strive.
roots_lines: Greek agon (G73) — a contest, the arena; Philippians 1:30, Colossians 2:1, 1 Timothy 6:12, 2 Timothy 4:7, Hebrews 12:1.
Greek agonizomai (G75) — to contend, strive; Colossians 4:12 of Epaphras labouring fervently in prayer.
Greek charizomai (G5483) — to give graciously; Philippians 1:29, it is given, from the same root as grace.
Greek sumbibazo (G4822) — to knit together; Colossians 2:2, the aim of Paul's conflict.
2 Timothy 4:7 uses the same noun at the end: I have fought a good fight — literally, I have contended the good contest.
usage: “Having the same conflict which ye saw in me” — apostle and congregation in one struggle.
“Unto you it is given… not only to believe on him, but also to suffer” — both are gifts.
“What great conflict I have for you… and for as many as have not seen my face”.

pos: v. (exerted oneself, made an earnest effort; of the response to the Macedonian vision, of longing to see a congregation, and of keeping the unity of the Spirit)
etymology: From endeavour, Old French en devoir, to put oneself in duty — to make it one's obligation. The Greek varies: zeteo, to seek, in Acts 16:10, and spoudazo, to be diligent or make haste, in Ephesians 4:3.
biblical_def: The word marks decisive obedience. After the vision at Troas: “And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them” (Acts 16:10). Two things stand out — the immediately, and the first appearance of we in Acts, marking where Luke joined the company. It also describes affection: “But we, brethren, being taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart, endeavoured the more abundantly to see your face with great desire” (1 Thessalonians 2:17). The most demanding use is a command: “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3). The Greek there is spoudazo, to make haste, to be diligent, and the object is not to create unity but to keep it — the unity already exists, made by the Spirit, and the labour is to preserve it. The ground follows immediately: “There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling” (Ephesians 4:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines endeavour as to exert physical strength or intellectual power for the accomplishment of an object, to try, to essay, to attempt.
webster_full: ENDEAVOR, v.i. To exert physical strength or intellectual power, for the accomplishment of an object; to try; to essay; to attempt.
ENDEAVOR, n. An effort; an essay; an attempt; an exertion of physical strength, or the intellectual powers, towards the attainment of an object.
DILIGENCE, n. Steady application in business of any kind; constant effort to accomplish what is undertaken.
UNITY, n. The state of being one; oneness; concord; conjunction.
BOND, n. That which binds; a band; a cord; a ligament.
scriptures: Ephesians 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
Acts 16:10
And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them.
Ephesians 4:4
There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling;
1 Thessalonians 2:17
But we, brethren, being taken from you for a short time in presence, not in heart, endeavoured the more abundantly to see your face with great desire.
corruption_summary: Unity is treated as something the church constructs by lowering doctrine, and Ephesians commands the keeping of a unity the Spirit already made.
corruption_paragraphs: The ecumenical use of Ephesians 4:3 reverses its grammar. The verse does not say endeavouring to achieve unity; it says to keep the unity of the Spirit, a unity that exists already because there is one body and one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. It is His work, not a negotiated settlement, and its basis is stated in the seven ones that follow — which are doctrinal, not merely relational. A movement that purchases visible agreement by suspending one faith has not kept the unity of the Spirit; it has traded the thing for a resemblance of it. Real unity is guarded by holding the confession, not by loosening it.

The command is nevertheless a hard one for those who see the point, because endeavouring translates a word meaning haste and diligence. Keeping unity is active work: swallowing an offence, seeking a brother out, refusing to circulate a grievance, bearing with a man whose manner is difficult. Ephesians 4:2 supplies the means immediately before — lowliness, meekness, longsuffering, forbearing one another in love. Doctrinal seriousness and this labour are not alternatives, and the Reformed churches, which have divided as often over temper as over truth, have particular reason to weigh the verse.
roots_summary: Greek spoudazo (G4704), to be diligent, make haste — Ephesians 4:3, 2 Peter 1:15, 2 Timothy 2:15; zeteo (G2212), to seek — Acts 16:10; spoudazo again in 1 Thessalonians 2:17.
roots_lines: Greek spoudazo (G4704) — to hasten, to be diligent; Ephesians 4:3, 1 Thessalonians 2:17, 2 Timothy 2:15, 2 Peter 1:15.
Greek zeteo (G2212) — to seek, to go about; Acts 16:10, of the immediate response to the vision.
Greek tereo (G5083) — to keep, guard, watch over; Ephesians 4:3 — the unity is kept, not made.
Greek sundesmos (G4886) — a joint band, a bond; Ephesians 4:3, the bond of peace.
Ephesians 4:4-6 supplies the seven grounds: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.
usage: “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit” — keep, not construct.
“Immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia” — and Luke joins the narrative here.
“Endeavoured the more abundantly to see your face with great desire”.

pos: n. (a running together, a gathering of people; the crowded place where Wisdom cries, and the unlawful assembly at Ephesus)
etymology: Latin concursus, a running together, from concurrere. The word describes movement before it describes a place — a concourse is where people converge, and only then a thoroughfare.
biblical_def: Wisdom is not portrayed in Proverbs as retiring or academic. She is in the street: “Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets: She crieth in the chief place of concourse, in the openings of the gates: in the city she uttereth her words” (Proverbs 1:20-21). The chief place of concourse is the busiest intersection in town, and the gates were where the elders sat and business was transacted. Wisdom takes her stand in the noisiest public place available and calls aloud. The other use is the aftermath of the Ephesian riot, in the town clerk's warning: “For we are in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar, there being no cause whereby we may give an account of this concourse” (Acts 19:40), after which “he dismissed the assembly” (Acts 19:41). His point is legal — an unlawful gathering with no stated cause exposed the whole city to Roman scrutiny. The two uses put the same kind of place to opposite uses: a crowd where wisdom cries, and a crowd where nobody knows why they came.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines concourse as a moving, flowing or running together, a meeting of persons, an assembly, and the place where a multitude meets.
webster_full: CONCOURSE, n. A moving, flowing or running together; confluence.
2. A meeting; an assembly of men; an assemblage of things; a collection formed by a voluntary or spontaneous moving and meeting in one place.
3. The place or point of meeting, or a place of frequent meeting.
THOROUGHFARE, n. A passage through; a passage from one street or opening to another.
GATE, n. The place of judgment; the place where courts were anciently held.
scriptures: Proverbs 1:21
She crieth in the chief place of concourse, in the openings of the gates: in the city she uttereth her words, saying,
Proverbs 1:20
Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets:
Acts 19:40
For we are in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar, there being no cause whereby we may give an account of this concourse.
Acts 19:41
And when he had thus spoken, he dismissed the assembly.
corruption_summary: Wisdom is imagined as private and specialised, and Proverbs puts her shouting at the busiest crossroads in the city.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 1:20-21 is a standing rebuke to two opposite instincts. The first treats wisdom as an interior, private possession — something cultivated in solitude and rarely spoken. The second treats it as technical, the property of specialists, unsuited to the street. Wisdom in Proverbs is in the street, at the gates, in the chief place of concourse, crying aloud where the traffic is heaviest, and the burden of her cry is that the simple may turn. Truth in Scripture is public by nature. The gospel was not preached in a corner, and a church that has no voice at the crossroads of its own town has misread the picture in the first chapter of Proverbs.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the contrast between the two concourses. In one, Wisdom cries and men refuse; the verses following are among the most solemn in the book — because I have called and ye refused, I also will laugh at your calamity. In the other, a whole city runs together for two hours and the greater part does not know why. Those are the two conditions of a crowd, and they are not far apart. The remedy in both cases is the same: a voice that says something definite, at the place where people actually are, and a hearing given to it before the season passes.
roots_summary: Hebrew homiyyoth, noisy or bustling places — Proverbs 1:21; Greek sustrophe (G4963), a twisting together, a riotous concourse — Acts 19:40, 23:12.
roots_lines: Hebrew homiyyoth — from hamah, to murmur or roar; the noisy chief places where Wisdom cries, Proverbs 1:21.
Hebrew shaar — a gate; the place of judgment and business, where the elders sat.
Greek sustrophe (G4963) — a banding together, a riotous gathering; Acts 19:40, and Acts 23:12 of the conspiracy against Paul.
Greek ekklesia (G1577) — assembly; Acts 19:41, dismissed by the town clerk.
Proverbs 1:24 records the response Wisdom met: because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded.
usage: “She crieth in the chief place of concourse, in the openings of the gates”.
“No cause whereby we may give an account of this concourse” — an assembly with no reason.
Two crowds: one where Wisdom cries, one where nobody knows why they came.
